title: The VUCA World Is Here - Systematic Investor - Ep.398

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The VUCA World Is Here - Systematic Investor - Ep.398.docx

summary: Systematic Investor, May 2026. Rzepczynski argues a VUCA, supply-shock world with ambiguity favours longer-lasting trends, and presents research that managed futures is insensitive to VIX risk regimes and shocks unlike other hedge fund strategies; discussion also covers replication, AI agents and narrative.

coverage.note: intro and VUCA framing, marathon record, robot half marathon, $6bn hedge fund redemption (chatter)
investor sophistication, Powell/Warsh Fed chair, UAE leaves OPEC, oil pipeline
April 2026 CTA strength, not just crisis alpha, Goldilocks crisis length, bank CTA flow forecasts
CTA fixed income short, Mimicking Finance AI replication
nonlinearity and breakout replication, replication versus best managers, correlation versus beta
alpha premium; index performance data; supply shock vs demand shock
1970s analogy, commodity shortages, undiscounted shock, WWI analogy
VIX falling, ambiguity slows decisions, slower systems do better
information processing, government intervention risk, 2020 policy
supply shock response creates inflation, hedge fund beta/alpha, VIX risk regimes
managed futures insensitive to risk regime and shocks, alternatives study update
crisis alpha beyond, global macro exceptions, story versus number
narrative context, NLP sentiment, price-only argument, multi-agent LLM
multi-agent analog, bundled versus pure strategies
multi-strat bundling, deep momentum bimodality, closing and plugs

completeness_estimate: 0.8 - the first reader caught the core ideas (Goldilocks crisis length, supply shock, ambiguity-slow-decision-trend link, VIX-regime study, replication and bundling debates); misses are secondary caveats, data points and the allocator-context and AI/LLM sub-points.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: what kind of Chairman Warsh will we have. Are you going to have the Warsh that's you know, sort of following a Trump lead of lowering interest rates
claims.claim: Market behaviour depends on whether the new Fed chair follows political pressure to cut rates or his earlier stance that the Fed balance sheet should shrink; a balance-sheet-shrinking chair would matter a lot for markets.
claims.indicator: Fed balance sheet, Fed chair stance
claims.testable: no: depends on future policy choices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the UAE um left OPEC. Um that's kind of an interesting um development as well because they're not a small member so to speak.
claims.claim: The UAE leaving OPEC, with a pipeline bypassing the Straits of Hormuz of about 1.5-2 million barrels a day, could mean more oil supply and more volatility in energy during the crisis, limited by pipeline capacity.
claims.testable: no: speculation about supply

correction.issue: Mixed attribution: Niels raises the UAE leaving OPEC and notes the pipeline limit, but the 1.5-2 million barrels a day pipeline figures (2 million reported, probably nearer 1.5) and the idea that the UAE will push out as much oil as it can during the crisis are Mark Rzepczynski's.
correction.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: the UAE leaving OPEC may mean more volatility in energy, but the pipeline physically limits how much more can be exported. Mark Rzepczynski: the UAE pipeline bypassing the Straits of Hormuz handles roughly 1.5 million barrels a day (2 million reported but likely high), so it will export as much as it can while the crisis lasts.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: people want to pin down the strategy as something like, "Oh, it's a crisis alpha." Or it only makes money when everything else goes pear-shaped.
claims.claim: Trend following is not only a crisis-alpha strategy: April 2026 was a strong CTA month with broad sector participation (energy dominant) even though equities had one of their best months in years.
claims.testable: yes: compare trend returns in up and down equity months

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the more that you have a length of some type of crisis, the longer the length and the crisis the time that we're in crisis, the better you'll be for a trend follower.
claims.claim: Goldilocks condition: crises that last longer give trend followers more time to capture trends; short sharp ones such as March 2020, which reversed within a month, hurt trend followers.
claims.direction: longer crisis is better for trend following
claims.conditions: crisis neither too short nor too long
claims.testable: yes: classify crisis length and measure trend returns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: all CTAs are going to buy 86 billion dollars worth of equity exposure in the next week, or they're going to sell.
claims.claim: Investment-bank estimates of CTA flows (such as Goldman's) are often inaccurate and not very useful, in the speaker's view, though they attract media attention.
claims.testable: yes: compare estimated flows with realised

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: fixed income positioning um did change in March um to the short side, and that we've kind of been building on that
claims.claim: CTA fixed-income positioning turned short in March 2026 on expected inflationary pressure from the Middle East conflict, in a sector that had been difficult with long/short exposure flipping every 6-8 weeks.
claims.conditions: sticks only if inflation pressure persists
claims.testable: partly: positioning is observable only with CTA data

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: they could get about 70% plus of the behavior of managers by using some AI agents to describe, you know, trading strategy and behavior.
claims.claim: Study 'Mimicking Finance': AI agents replicate about 70% of portfolio-manager behaviour, but performance falls below the best managers, who are more dynamic and rule-rich and hard to mimic.
claims.indicator: AI agent replication of manager behaviour
claims.testable: yes: published replication study

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I wonder if do you really need an AI nowadays to do that if you can just look up the replicators positions in the ETF space every single day.
claims.claim: Replicating trend followers with AI is unnecessary when daily positions of trend replication ETFs are public.
claims.testable: no: opinion

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: The hard part is is that when you think about a lot of managers use breakout systems. A breakout system is somewhat nonlinear in the sense is that you're dormant until you see a move in the market
claims.claim: Trend replication struggles with nonlinear, threshold-based signals (breakouts: dormant until a move passes a threshold) while moving-average strategies are easy to replicate.
claims.testable: yes: replicate each signal type and compare

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think we as an industry have moved towards more continuous signaling.
claims.claim: Most larger CTAs have moved from breakout triggers to continuous signals, while some smaller managers use breakouts with static position sizing and have had outsized returns in 2026.
claims.testable: partly: depends on manager data

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: just because the performance looks the same, it must be the same. But this is where I just don't think that is true
claims.claim: A 0.75-0.8 correlation between a replicator and trend managers does not prove replication works; the replicator has shown more downside volatility and drawdown than the equivalent fund and has not beaten the best managers.
claims.testable: yes: compare drawdown and downside risk

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you could have a pretty high correlation but that does but you could still have a negative beta relative to the managers set
claims.claim: Correlation is a poor guide to replication quality: a replicator can be highly correlated yet have a negative beta to the managers it targets.
claims.testable: yes: regression of replicator on managers

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: it's that alpha component that is the intangible that's not being picked up by some factors which is you can't replicate and is also what people are will be paying a premium for
claims.claim: The alpha component not captured by simple factors cannot be replicated and is what investors pay fees for.
claims.testable: no: argument about fees and alpha

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer yesterday closed at 55. So, that's pretty solid and I think that reflects well the performance we're seeing at the moment
claims.claim: Trend barometer reading 55 on 28 April 2026 matches a strong trend-following month: BTOP50 +1.84% April and +9.46% YTD, SG CTA +9.92%, SG Trend +9.71%, Brevan Howard flat-fee trend index +12.39%, S&P 500 TR +4.63% YTD.
claims.indicator: trend barometer, BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, Brevan Howard index
claims.testable: yes: published index returns

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: it is a supply shock and we'll sort of say that the global economy has a difficulty with supply shocks over demand shocks.
claims.claim: Supply shocks (such as the oil shock from the Middle East conflict) are harder for central banks than demand shocks, since cutting rates to boost demand worsens inflation; this leaves policy unsure and prices free to trend.
claims.indicator: oil price shock, Eurozone inflation about 3%, US inflation above 2%
claims.conditions: supply shock with inflation above target
claims.testable: partly: classify shocks as supply or demand

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: that gives us into more of a 70s kind of world. But, if you have a 70s type world, then you could be able to have extended price trends across many different markets.
claims.claim: A persistent supply-shock inflation regime resembles the 1970s and produces extended price trends across many markets, including fertilizer, propane, butane and refined products affected by the closed Straits of Hormuz.
claims.indicator: fertilizer, propane, butane, refined product shortages
claims.testable: partly: analog-period study

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: there's not been the proper discounting of this this large event.
claims.claim: Equities held up and VIX fell despite the energy shock, so the event may not be discounted; as in July 1914 when equity markets were surprised by war, equities may be surprised by the Middle East escalation.
claims.testable: partly: historical analogy only

correction.issue: Date error: the transcript does not say July 1914. Mark asks what equity markets did after the Archduke was shot and before September 1914, before all-out war, and says they did not discount the war and were completely surprised.
correction.fix: Mark Rzepczynski: equities held up and VIX fell despite the energy shock, so the event may not be discounted; as in the weeks after the Archduke's assassination and before September 1914, when equity markets did not discount war and were completely surprised, equities may be surprised by the Middle East escalation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the initial inflation period is not necessarily bad
claims.claim: Higher inflation leading to higher rates and lower equities tends to play out with a lag; the initial inflation period is not necessarily bad for equities.
claims.testable: yes: lagged return regression on inflation shocks

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: in an ambiguous world, a world with high uncertainty, the normal expected behavior, which is going to be good for trend following, is is that uh everyone is going to slow down with their decision-making.
claims.claim: High ambiguity and conflicting signals make investors slow down, dollar-cost average and delay action, which spreads decisions over time and produces longer price trends.
claims.testable: partly: uncertainty indices vs trend returns

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: The daily uncertainty indices have been very volatile
claims.claim: Uncertainty indices are high but may have peaked, while VIX has declined over the last eight or so weeks to only slightly above median, suggesting investors are numb to news.
claims.indicator: VIX, daily and monthly uncertainty indices
claims.testable: yes: published series

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It's actually the slower systems, the slower models, that are better at navigating the environment.
claims.claim: Despite instant information distribution, slower trend models have navigated markets better than shorter-term models in recent years, which is counterintuitive.
claims.testable: yes: compare speeds over time

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: Our our ability to gain information is better than ever in the past. Is our but our ability to process that information may not have improved.
claims.claim: Information is abundant but human processing ability has not improved, so uncertainty and behaviour can lead to trends lasting longer than expected, favouring longer trends over high-frequency edge.
claims.testable: partly: hard to form a direct hypothesis

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the worst fear of a trend follower is is is that the trend start to occur and then government policy comes in and arrests the trends or tries to reverse it.
claims.claim: Government intervention is the main risk to trends; in a supply shock the proper policy response is unclear, so prices are driven by market behaviour rather than policy.
claims.conditions: supply shock, no clear policy response
claims.testable: partly: identify intervention episodes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that suddenly led to some reversals and some trends that changed direction. But, it also led to one of the strongest periods for trend following subsequently.
claims.claim: Fed intervention in March 2020 caused reversals but was followed by one of the strongest periods for trend following because the stimulus proved very inflationary.
claims.testable: partly: single episode

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: by offsetting the supply shock, then they actually created a bigger problem, which actually led to inflation, which then led to, you know, advantages for trend followers.
claims.claim: Governments offset the pandemic supply shock with fiscal spending, low rates and liquidity, which generated inflation and then benefitted trend followers.
claims.testable: partly: single episode

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the standard argument is is that the beta for trend following is close to zero. And so it's it's is it's a very low number.
claims.claim: Trend following has near-zero equity beta and near-zero alpha in simple regressions, while other hedge fund strategies have positive beta and some significant positive alpha, so trend gives diversification but little alpha.
claims.indicator: regression beta and alpha of hedge fund strategies
claims.testable: yes: regression of HFRI strategy indices

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: in high risk regimes, this is that there is a negative well, the coefficient is is
claims.claim: Most hedge fund strategies have a negative coefficient on high-VIX risk regimes (lower excess returns when VIX is high), unlike low-risk regimes.
claims.indicator: VIX risk regime coefficient on hedge fund strategy excess returns
claims.testable: yes: regression on standardized VIX

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: when you look at managed futures, they're actually uh in a insensitive to the risk regime. So, whether it's high risk or low risk, that coefficient is not significant.
claims.claim: Managed futures returns are insensitive to the VIX risk regime (coefficient not significant), and alpha of other strategies turns negative in the high-VIX tercile while managed futures stays invariant.
claims.direction: managed futures preferred when worried about volatility
claims.testable: yes: partition by VIX terciles

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: most hedge fund strategies don't really do well with positive risk shocks. On the other hand, managed futures, again, seems to be invariant to risk shocks.
claims.claim: Risk shocks, measured as the change in VIX, hurt most hedge fund strategies but not managed futures, giving a diversification advantage beyond low beta.
claims.testable: yes: regress returns on VIX change

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we looked at all the alternative investment strategies we could get our data on. I think there's like 14 or 16 of them.
claims.claim: A comparable study of 14-16 alternative strategies since 2000, the start of the trend index, has been updated and will be published in a weekly email.
claims.testable: yes: study already run

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: it's hard to find hedge fund strategies that do well in a positive risk shock or a high volatility regime. But you do have you know, some exceptions and that's managed futures.
claims.claim: Few hedge fund strategies do well in high volatility or positive risk shocks; managed futures and global macro (similar but one systematic, one discretionary) are the exceptions.
claims.testable: yes: strategy returns vs VIX

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: No one ever made a decision because of a number. They need a story.
claims.claim: Investors want a story, which is a constant marketing challenge for trend followers who say only 'prices go up, I buy'; managers with narrative context may win allocations.
claims.testable: no: behavioural marketing point

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we could take uh you know, earnings calls, and we could be able to use what is called a bag of words, and then be able to try to figure out the
claims.claim: NLP sentiment from earnings calls (bag of words) is profitable in equities, but how to use it in a trend following model is not yet researched.
claims.testable: yes: sentiment signals can be tested

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: those managers who've just stuck with using price um has actually done very well.
claims.claim: Managers who stuck to price-only trend following have done very well across decades of change, and added context (sentiment, economic trend) is not clearly better.
claims.testable: yes: compare price-only versus augmented trend models

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if you have an uh model that has an agent, one is following technical signals, another one is looking at fundamentals, another one is looking at sentiment, and then you
claims.claim: Multi-agent LLM systems that ensemble technical, fundamental and sentiment agents show better Sharpe ratios than single-agent models.
claims.indicator: multi-agent ensemble of technical, fundamental, sentiment signals
claims.testable: yes: compare ensemble to single agent out of sample

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: when you think about a manager that uses a number of different strategies, he's acting like a multi-agent LLM.
claims.claim: Blending trend with other strategies in one manager resembles a multi-agent ensemble; the open question is whether to buy pure strategies and blend them or buy the bundle.
claims.testable: partly: compare bundled versus component portfolios

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: using more things is potentially better. I just think it's an easy narrative, right? Because it could also be much more confusing.
claims.claim: The narrative that using more inputs improves trend following is easy but may add confusion (strong GDP data while markets fall); a narrow price-only approach continues to work.
claims.testable: partly: test added fundamentals against price-only baseline

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we have maybe you know, hundreds of pods. What they're saying is that all those pods are supposed to be orthogonal.
claims.claim: Multi-strategy platforms sell bundling hundreds of orthogonal pods with faster risk management, the same bundle-versus-component choice investors face.
claims.testable: no: business model description

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you'll have some past winners that continue to win which is what you'd expect in momentum but then you have some past winners that lose really bad.
claims.claim: Deep-momentum research on bimodality finds past winners split into continuing winners and big losers, offering an explanation of momentum crashes.
claims.indicator: bimodal distribution of past winners (deep momentum)
claims.testable: yes: cross-sectional return distribution of winners

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we're living in a VUCA world now, and, and I think that's going to be what our, our discussion, for the most part, is
claims.claim: The current environment is a VUCA world (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity) in uncharted territory, and the practical question for a quant investor is how to navigate it, which frames the later argument that ambiguity favours trends.
claims.conditions: regime with high uncertainty and ambiguity
claims.testable: partly - VUCA is a framing; uncertainty indices could proxy it

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: investors have become more and more sophisticated. And as their sophistication has increased, they demand more from the managers that they invest with
claims.claim: Allocators have become steadily more sophisticated and demand more from managers, so competition is both across firms and in meeting investor expectations, which are now high.
claims.testable: no - qualitative industry observation

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I would not be surprised if the SocGen Trend Index makes a new all-time high
claims.claim: On the last trading day of April 2026 the SG Trend Index and many CTAs looked set to end the month at new all-time highs, recovering fully from the drawdown despite the turbulence.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index level vs prior peak
claims.testable: yes - index history

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: March was certainly a month where uh we had to trim uh equity exposure because of the reversals
claims.claim: After the surprise Middle East attack, March 2026 forced CTAs to trim equity exposure on reversals: some managers got out almost completely or slightly short, while many longer-term trend followers stayed long, so slower systems took less damage.
claims.indicator: CTA equity exposure by trend speed
claims.direction: short-term systems cut equities, long-term systems stayed long
claims.conditions: sharp equity reversal on geopolitical shock
claims.testable: yes - compare fast vs slow trend systems in March 2026

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: prime brokers, brokers in general have four decades been trying to reverse engineer trend following programs
claims.claim: Reverse-engineering trend programs from their behaviour is not new (brokers have tried for four decades); what is new is the use of AI to do it.
claims.testable: no - historical context

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: what happens when we add more complexity to models is do we really get an advantage
claims.claim: Whether extra model complexity (AI agents able to include nonlinearities) actually improves replication of trend following over simpler replication is an open empirical question that must be tested against the simple replicator.
claims.indicator: AI-agent replicator vs simple replicator tracking error
claims.testable: yes - out-of-sample tracking of target managers

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's not the best indices that I could think of if you want to compare yourself to that and some Morningstar type trend following or a systematic
claims.claim: Comparing a replicator's returns with broad Morningstar-type trend or systematic indices is not the right benchmark; the comparison should be with like-for-like funds.
claims.testable: yes - recompute replicator excess return against alternative benchmarks

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: replication in the relatively short period it's been around has kept up uh overall performance-wise and and in some cases also outperform um the indices
claims.claim: Replication products have, over their short history, kept pace with trend indices and sometimes beaten them, which the speaker concedes while arguing they have not beaten the best managers.
claims.testable: yes - fund and index returns

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: There were some reversals at different times based on comments that were made. But, surprisingly is this is that the markets has stayed higher.
claims.claim: Because the Middle East event keeps extending, dislocations have stronger and longer effects that show up in prices: oil reversed repeatedly on headlines yet stayed higher, so a trader long from early March did reasonably well despite higher volatility.
claims.indicator: crude oil price trend after March 2026 shock
claims.testable: yes - oil trend system P&L March-April 2026

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: I know we just had the Eurozone inflation. It's coming in about 3%.
claims.claim: Euro-area inflation is about 3% and US inflation stays persistently above 2% (trimmed-mean view), which leaves central banks without a clear response to the supply shock and supports the 1970s-style regime argument.
claims.testable: yes - official inflation series

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the S&P 500 total return up a whopping 9.37% in April and up 4.63% so far this year
claims.claim: In April 2026 equities surged (MSCI World +8.35%, S&P 500 TR +9.37%) while trend indices gained only about 2.3-2.5%, short-term traders +0.56% and US aggregate bonds were flat, so the trend gain came from non-equity sectors rather than from an equity crash.
claims.indicator: MSCI World, S&P 500 TR, S&P US Aggregate, SG CTA/Trend/Short-Term Traders, April 2026
claims.testable: yes - index data

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: when you ever say a market is not discounting the markets, it means that you have an opinion
claims.claim: Saying a market is not discounting an event is itself a directional opinion, not evidence, so the claim that equities have not priced the Middle East shock needs a test rather than assertion.
claims.testable: no - epistemic caveat

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: inelastic is is not so much is is is due to the behavior and flow of markets
claims.claim: The inelastic market hypothesis is about market behaviour and flows, which is a different argument from the supply-shock point that governments do not know how to arrest the trend.
claims.testable: partly - inelastic-markets literature has flow-price tests, but not tied to the supply-shock claim here

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you're not competing against other trend followers, you're competing against all other hedge fund strategies
claims.claim: Institutional allocators choose trend following against all other hedge fund strategies that might diversify, not only against other trend followers, so its case must be made relative to the whole alternatives menu.
claims.testable: partly - allocator surveys, not a market signal

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: how do we process a lot of information, some of which is non-numerical, in a way that we can then be able to and convert into signals
claims.claim: Besides NLP sentiment, large language models are the second main AI use in quant research, converting non-numerical information into trading signals that could add context to models.
claims.testable: yes - test the LLM signal's incremental value over price trend

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of this sentiment and so on and so forth should all be reflected in the price, and the price is the only truth that we have
claims.claim: Sentiment and similar context should already be reflected in prices, which are the only hard truth, so price-only trend following remains potent and extra context is not obviously better.
claims.testable: yes - incremental value of sentiment over price trend

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: finding a pure trend following manager it there are fewer of those and more of them try to mix and match in a sort of other types of strategies within that
claims.claim: Pure trend-following managers are becoming rarer as most add other strategy types, a drift the host expects may leave even fewer pure trend followers in five years, though it could reverse.
claims.testable: partly - manager database classification over time

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's good bundling and bad bundling and sometimes we we may not know what is good or bad bundling until after the fact
claims.claim: Bundled products (multi-strat, structured packages) can be good or bad, and the investor often cannot tell which until afterwards (the bundled bad loans of 2008 being the cautionary example), so bundling needs ex-ante scrutiny.
claims.testable: no - qualitative judgement
